questions.stem: The Decree on Land issued on 26 October 1917:
options: turned every peasant farm into a state collective run by party officials
returned confiscated land to the nobility in exchange for their loyalty
granted land only to peasants who had joined the Bolshevik party
abolished private landownership and gave estates to peasant committees
questions.explanation: The decree abolished private ownership of land without compensation and left the redistribution of noble, Church and crown estates to local land committees and soviets. It largely approved seizures peasants had already made; collectivisation came only under Stalin.

questions.stem: In the first weeks after October 1917, the Sovnarkom faced which immediate problem?
options: an armed revolt of the Left SRs, who had refused to cooperate with the soviets at all
a demand by Nicholas II, still in Petrograd, to be restored to the throne by the army
a strike by state employees and the railway union's demand for an all-socialist coalition
an invasion of Petrograd by Japanese troops landed from the Pacific coast in November
questions.explanation: Civil servants and bank staff refused to work for the new government, and the railway workers' union, Vikzhel, threatened a strike unless a coalition of all socialist parties was formed. The Left SRs in fact joined the Sovnarkom in December; their revolt came only in July 1918.

questions.stem: The Bolshevik Decree on the Press of 27 October 1917 allowed the government to:
options: close newspapers hostile to the new regime
guarantee complete freedom of the press to all parties
hand all printing presses to the Orthodox Church
fund independent newspapers for the Kadet party
questions.explanation: The decree, presented as temporary, let the government shut down 'counter-revolutionary' papers, and the Kadet and other opposition press was soon closed. It is an early sign that civil liberties would be limited to defend the revolution.

questions.stem: Which group of early Soviet decrees best shows an attempt to change Russia's social structure?
options: abolishing ranks and titles, separating Church and state, allowing civil marriage
restoring the Table of Ranks, making Orthodoxy the state faith and banning divorce
returning estates to nobles, raising redemption payments and banning trade unions
reviving the Duma, confirming the Fundamental Laws and protecting noble titles
questions.explanation: Decrees of late 1917 and early 1918 abolished estates and civil ranks, separated Church from state and school, and made marriage a civil matter with easier divorce. The other options describe the old order the decrees were dismantling.

questions.stem: The Cheka, set up in December 1917 to fight counter-revolution and sabotage, was headed by:
options: Nikolai Bukharin
Grigory Zinoviev
Felix Dzerzhinsky
Leon Trotsky
questions.explanation: Dzerzhinsky, a Polish-born revolutionary, led the Cheka from its creation and built it into a powerful political police force. Trotsky led the Red Army as Commissar for War.

questions.stem: A historian argues that the Cheka showed continuity with Tsarist rule. Which evidence best supports this argument?
options: Like the Okhrana, it used secret police methods against political opponents
It answered to the Constituent Assembly as the Tsar's ministers had answered to the Duma
It enforced the freedoms of speech and assembly that the October Manifesto had promised
It was disbanded once the Civil War began, as the Okhrana had been disbanded in 1905
questions.explanation: The Cheka, like the Tsarist Okhrana, used surveillance, informers, arrest and exile against opponents, though on a far larger and more violent scale. It answered to the party leadership rather than any elected body, and it grew stronger during the Civil War.

questions.stem: In the Constituent Assembly elections of November 1917, the party that won the most seats was:
options: the Constitutional Democrats (Kadets)
the Mensheviks
the Socialist Revolutionaries
the Bolsheviks
questions.explanation: The SRs, with their peasant support, won the largest share of seats; the Bolsheviks came second, strong in the cities and the army. This result was a problem for a government that claimed to rule in the people's name.

questions.stem: Lenin defended the dissolution of the Constituent Assembly mainly by arguing that:
options: the Assembly had voted to restore the monarchy under Grand Duke Michael
the Bolsheviks had in fact won an outright majority of its seats
the Allies had demanded that it be closed as a condition of their aid
soviets were a higher form of democracy than a bourgeois parliament
questions.explanation: Lenin claimed the Assembly reflected outdated party lists drawn up before the SR split and that the soviets of workers, soldiers and peasants were a truer expression of the people's will. The Assembly had no monarchist majority, and the Bolsheviks won about a quarter of the seats, not a majority.

questions.stem: The Treaty of Brest-Litovsk, signed on 3 March 1918, ended Russia's war with:
options: Germany and its allies, at the cost of vast territory
Japan, which returned Port Arthur to Russian control
Poland, fixing a new border well to the east of Warsaw
Britain and France, ending their military intervention
questions.explanation: Brest-Litovsk took Russia out of the First World War on very harsh German terms. The border with Poland was fixed later by the Treaty of Riga (1921), after the Polish–Soviet War.

questions.stem: Under the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk, Russia gave up control of:
options: the Crimea, the Ural Mountains and western Siberia
Ukraine, Finland, Poland and the Baltic lands
Central Asia, Siberia and the Pacific coast
Moscow, Petrograd and the Volga provinces
questions.explanation: Russia lost its western borderlands, which held a large share of its population, farmland, coal and industry. Moscow and Petrograd stayed Soviet, although the government moved the capital to Moscow in March 1918 for safety.

questions.stem: At Brest-Litovsk, Trotsky's policy of 'neither war nor peace' failed because:
options: the Red Army defeated Germany and forced new negotiations
Germany resumed its advance and then imposed harsher terms
the Allies landed in Petrograd to keep Russia in the war
the Left SRs signed their own separate treaty with Austria
questions.explanation: Trotsky refused to sign but declared the war over, hoping revolution in Germany would rescue Russia. The German army advanced rapidly in February 1918, and Lenin forced the party to accept worse terms than those first offered.

questions.stem: Bukharin and the Left Communists opposed the Brest-Litovsk treaty, while Lenin insisted on signing it. Which statement best captures Lenin's reasoning?
options: Peace bought a breathing space for the regime to survive until revolution spread
A revolutionary war would spread socialism to Germany's workers within months
The Allies had promised to recover all the lost lands for Russia after the war
Giving up the borderlands would free the Soviets from depending on their grain
questions.explanation: Lenin argued that the army could not fight and that the revolution's survival came first, even at a terrible price. Revolutionary war to spread revolution was the Left Communists' position, which Lenin rejected as reckless.

questions.stem: As Commissar for War, Trotsky strengthened the Red Army by:
options: abolishing all ranks and letting the soldiers elect their own officers by vote
relying entirely on volunteer Red Guard units recruited in the factories
hiring German officers released under the terms of Brest-Litovsk
conscripting soldiers and using former Tsarist officers watched by commissars
questions.explanation: Trotsky replaced elected officers and volunteers with conscription, harsh discipline and thousands of 'military specialists' from the Tsarist army, supervised by political commissars. Electing officers was a 1917 practice he reversed.

questions.stem: Which factor best explains the Reds' victory in the Civil War?
options: They held the central heartland and railways while the Whites were divided and scattered
The Allied powers sent large armies to fight on the Bolshevik side against the Whites
The peasants backed the Whites, whose generals promised to protect their land seizures
The Whites refused all foreign supplies and had no officers with military training
questions.explanation: The Reds controlled Moscow, Petrograd, the main railways and much industry, and had a single command; the Whites fought on separate fronts, distrusted each other and were linked to the return of landlords. The Allies supplied the Whites, not the Reds.

questions.stem: The Red Terror was officially declared in September 1918, following:
options: an attempt on Lenin's life and the killing of Uritsky
the Kronstadt sailors' revolt against Bolshevik rule in Petrograd
the signing of the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk
the death of Lenin and the struggle to succeed him
questions.explanation: After Fanya Kaplan shot and wounded Lenin and the Petrograd Cheka chief Uritsky was assassinated in August 1918, the government authorised mass arrests, hostage-taking and executions of 'class enemies'. Kronstadt came in 1921 and Lenin died in 1924.

questions.stem: The 'White Terror' of the Civil War refers to:
options: the shelling of the Winter Palace by the cruiser Aurora in October 1917
violence by anti-Bolshevik forces against suspected Reds, Jews and peasants
the Cheka's executions of nobles, priests and officers in the major cities
the famine that struck the Volga region at the end of the Civil War in 1921
questions.explanation: White forces carried out executions of suspected Bolsheviks, reprisals against villages and, especially in Ukraine, pogroms against Jews. The Cheka's executions were the Red Terror.

questions.stem: In State and Revolution (1917), Lenin argued that under communism the state would wither away. Which development of 1918–21 best shows this ideal being compromised?
options: The growth of the Cheka and a centralised one-party state
The Decree on Land that gave estates to the peasants
The Treaty of Riga that ended the Polish–Soviet War
The adoption of the Western Gregorian calendar
questions.explanation: Instead of withering away, the state grew more centralised and coercive, with the Cheka, banned opposition parties and power concentrated in the Communist Party. The Decree on Land fulfilled a promise rather than compromising one.

questions.stem: State Capitalism, from late 1917 to mid-1918, involved:
options: state control of banks and key industries while small businesses stayed private
nationalisation of every enterprise in Russia down to the smallest workshop
the abolition of money and a total ban on private trade across all of Russia
the return of nationalised factories to their pre-war owners without conditions
questions.explanation: Lenin saw State Capitalism as a transition: banks were nationalised, Vesenkha was set up to oversee the economy, and many managers and small businesses carried on under state supervision. Full nationalisation and the ban on private trade came with War Communism.

questions.stem: Which feature belonged to War Communism rather than to State Capitalism?
options: Keeping bourgeois managers under state supervision
Leaving most small enterprises in private hands
Nationalising the banks while leaving trade free
Forced requisitioning of grain from the peasants
questions.explanation: War Communism, from mid-1918, brought grain requisitioning, nationalisation of nearly all industry, a ban on private trade and labour conscription. Keeping specialists and private small firms was typical of the earlier, more moderate State Capitalism.

questions.stem: Under War Communism, grain requisitioning (prodrazvyorstka) meant that:
options: the state bought grain from the kulaks at prices set by the free market
grain was exported to Germany to pay for the Red Army's weapons
armed detachments seized peasants' surplus grain for the towns and army
peasants paid a fixed tax in kind and sold the rest of their grain freely
questions.explanation: Food detachments and the Committees of Poor Peasants took grain beyond the peasants' bare needs, often by force, paying little or nothing. A fixed tax in kind with free sale of the surplus was the NEP that replaced requisitioning in 1921.

questions.stem: The Kronstadt sailors who rebelled in March 1921 demanded:
options: a new declaration of war against Imperial Germany
newly elected soviets and free speech for socialist parties
the restoration of the Tsar and of the Orthodox Church
the return of the noble estates confiscated in 1917
questions.explanation: The Petropavlovsk resolution called for re-elections to the soviets by secret ballot, freedom of speech and press for workers, peasants and left socialist parties, and an end to grain requisitioning. Its demands were for soviet democracy, not a return to the old order.

questions.stem: Alongside the New Economic Policy, the Tenth Party Congress of March 1921:
options: reopened the Constituent Assembly in Petrograd
legalised the Menshevik and SR parties again
abolished the Cheka and released its prisoners
banned factions within the Communist Party
questions.explanation: The resolution 'On Party Unity' forbade organised groups inside the party, so criticism of the leadership could be treated as factionalism. Rival parties remained suppressed and the Cheka continued.

questions.stem: The Workers' Opposition, led by Shlyapnikov and Kollontai and condemned at the Tenth Party Congress, had demanded that:
options: the Communist Party should share power with the Mensheviks
trade unions rather than party officials should run industry
the NEP's private trade should be extended to heavy industry
the Red Army should take over the management of factories
questions.explanation: The Workers' Opposition argued that the workers' own unions should manage production, protesting at bureaucracy and one-man management. Putting the economy under military-style control was closer to Trotsky's militarisation of labour, which they opposed.

questions.stem: The famine of 1921, centred on the Volga region, was made far worse by:
options: the NEP's ban on peasants trading grain in the markets
the Treaty of Riga's transfer of the Volga to Poland
Stolypin's resettlement of Volga peasants in Siberia
drought coming on top of years of grain requisitioning
questions.explanation: A severe drought struck a countryside already stripped of reserves by requisitioning and war, leaving peasants with no stocks to survive on. The NEP allowed rather than banned the private sale of grain.

questions.stem: Under the New Economic Policy, peasants:
options: had all their grain beyond bare subsistence seized by armed squads
were made to join collective farms run by the state
were made to resume redemption payments for land
paid a tax in kind and could sell their surplus privately
questions.explanation: The NEP replaced requisitioning with a tax in kind, later paid in money, and let peasants trade the rest. This restored incentives to grow food and calmed the peasant revolts of 1920–21.

questions.stem: Under the NEP, the 'commanding heights' that stayed under state control were:
options: newspapers, theatres and the churches
village communes, markets and cooperatives
heavy industry, banking and foreign trade
small workshops, retail shops and farms
questions.explanation: The state kept large-scale industry, the banks and foreign trade, while small factories, retail trade and agriculture were returned to private hands. This mixed economy was Lenin's 'strategic retreat'.

questions.stem: In 1923, prices of manufactured goods rose well above agricultural prices, opening the 'scissors crisis'. This threatened the NEP mainly because:
options: factories had to close because grain had become too costly to buy
the state was obliged to return to requisitioning the same month
Nepmen were forbidden by law from trading in grain and cloth
peasants had little reason to sell grain when it bought so few goods
questions.explanation: When grain bought few manufactured goods, peasants held back from the market, threatening food supplies to the towns. Grain was cheap, not costly, which is what made the gap between the two price 'blades' so damaging.

questions.stem: In 1925 Bukharin urged the peasants to 'enrich yourselves'. Which view of the NEP does this best illustrate?
options: Large industry should be handed back to its private owners
Peasant prosperity under the NEP could build socialism gradually
The NEP was a brief retreat to be ended within a few months
The kulaks should be eliminated as a class without delay
questions.explanation: Bukharin, the NEP's leading defender, believed that prosperous peasants buying goods would fund industry and that socialism could grow slowly through the market. The call to eliminate the kulaks belongs to Stalin's later policy of collectivisation.

questions.stem: The Proletkult movement aimed to:
options: revive Orthodox religious music in the new working-class districts
create a new proletarian culture made by workers themselves
preserve the art of the Tsarist court in state museums
train former Tsarist officers to serve in the Red Army
questions.explanation: Proletkult, led by Alexander Bogdanov, set up studios and clubs where workers would create a culture free of bourgeois influence. Lenin distrusted its independence and brought it under the Commissariat of Enlightenment.

questions.stem: Vladimir Tatlin's design for the Monument to the Third International is associated with:
options: Romanticism
Constructivism
Socialist Realism
Impressionism
questions.explanation: Constructivists such as Tatlin and Rodchenko used industrial materials and geometric forms to make art serve the new society. Socialist Realism became the compulsory style only in the 1930s under Stalin, after this period of experimentation.

questions.stem: The Bolshevik literacy campaign (likbez) and the rabfaks (workers' faculties) aimed mainly to:
options: return schools and universities to the control of the Orthodox Church
replace Russian with the languages of the minorities in all schools
spread literacy and bring workers and peasants into higher education
limit schooling and universities to the children of party members
questions.explanation: A 1919 decree required illiterate adults to learn to read, and the rabfaks prepared workers and peasants for university. Under Lunacharsky's Commissariat of Enlightenment, schooling was separated from the Church, not returned to it.

questions.stem: Alexandra Kollontai is best known in this period as:
options: the White leader who commanded the Volunteer Army in southern Russia
the Commissar for War who organised the defence of Petrograd in 1919
a Bolshevik leader who championed women's rights and social welfare
the head of the Cheka who organised the Red Terror against opponents
questions.explanation: Kollontai was People's Commissar for Social Welfare in the first Soviet government and later led the Zhenotdel, the party's women's department. She argued that socialism must free women from domestic drudgery and the traditional family.

questions.stem: Which change for women came in the first years of Soviet rule?
options: church weddings as the only legal form of marriage
the removal of women's right to vote in the soviets
civil marriage, easier divorce and legal abortion
a ban on women working in factories and offices
questions.explanation: Decrees and the 1918 Family Code made marriage a civil matter and divorce simple, and abortion was legalised in 1920. These were among the most radical family laws in the world at the time.

questions.stem: Historians often argue that women's equality changed more on paper than in practice in the 1920s. Which evidence best supports this view?
options: Women still did most domestic work and were often first to lose jobs under the NEP
Women were barred from joining the Communist Party until the late 1920s
The Zhenotdel was abolished within a year of its creation in 1919
The 1918 Family Code restored a husband's legal authority over his wife
questions.explanation: Despite the new laws, women carried a double burden of paid work and housework, and women were often among the first dismissed as unemployment rose under the NEP. The Zhenotdel lasted until 1930, and the Family Code made spouses legally equal.

questions.stem: Under the 1918 Constitution of the Russian Soviet Republic, people who lived on unearned income or hired labour for profit:
options: were guaranteed seats in the Sovnarkom
were denied the right to vote
were given extra votes in elections
were made managers of nationalised factories
questions.explanation: The constitution disenfranchised former exploiters, including merchants, landlords living on rent, clergy and former police. This made the bourgeoisie and nobility second-class citizens in the new state.

questions.stem: Which development of 1918–21 most clearly shows factory workers' hopes of 1917 being compromised?
options: The Decree on Land gave noble estates to the peasants and not the workers
The eight-hour day was decreed for all workers in October 1917
Factory committees were elected across Petrograd during 1917
Workers' control gave way to one-man management and labour discipline
questions.explanation: In 1917 workers hoped to run their factories through elected committees, but the regime soon restored managers, piece rates and harsh discipline, and Trotsky proposed militarising labour. The eight-hour day and factory committees were gains of 1917, not compromises.

questions.stem: By 1927, which statement best describes the peasants' position compared with 1917?
options: Most farmed land they had seized, largely within revived village communes
Most worked on state collective farms under managers sent by the party
Most rented their land back from nobles who had returned from exile
Most had resumed redemption payments abolished before the war began
questions.explanation: The land seizures of 1917–18 were confirmed, and under the NEP the traditional mir revived as peasants farmed small family plots. Collectivisation began only from 1929, and redemption payments were never restored.

questions.stem: A historian argues that Soviet Russia in 1927 showed strong continuity with Tsarism. Which pair of features best supports this?
options: Rule by one party without elected checks, enforced by a political police
A free press and an elected national parliament with power over ministers
Private ownership of large industry and of the great landed estates
An official state church and hereditary titles for the governing class
questions.explanation: Like the autocracy, the Communist Party ruled without a freely elected parliament and relied on a secret police to suppress opposition. Private estates, a state church and hereditary titles had all been abolished, so these marked change rather than continuity.

questions.stem: Lenin's 'Testament' of 1922–23 warned the party about Stalin and recommended that he be:
options: put in charge of the Cheka
removed from the post of General Secretary
made the next chairman of the Council of People's Commissars
given command of the Red Army
questions.explanation: In a postscript of January 1923 Lenin called Stalin too rude and urged comrades to find a way to remove him as General Secretary. The Testament was not acted on after Lenin's death in January 1924, and Stalin went on to defeat his rivals.

questions.stem: By the end of 1927, Leon Trotsky had been:
options: expelled from the Communist Party
made chairman of the Sovnarkom
appointed head of the secret police
elected General Secretary of the party
questions.explanation: Trotsky lost the power struggle after Lenin's death, was removed as Commissar for War in 1925 and expelled from the party in 1927, then exiled. His defeat marked Stalin's rise as the NEP drew to a close.

questions.stem: Sheila Fitzpatrick's The Russian Revolution treats the revolution as:
options: a foreign plot organised and paid for by the German government
a process running from 1917 through to Stalin's revolution of the 1930s
a single event that was completed on the night of 25 October 1917
a coup that Lenin came to regret and then reversed through the NEP
questions.explanation: Fitzpatrick argues that the revolution unfolded over many years, with Stalin's industrialisation and collectivisation as its final, violent phase. This places October 1917 at the start of a long process rather than as a single moment.

questions.stem: Richard Pipes argued that Stalinism:
options: marked a return to the liberal reforms of Stolypin
grew directly out of Lenin's methods and institutions
betrayed a democratic Leninism that worked well until 1924
was imposed on Russia by the hostile Western powers
questions.explanation: Pipes saw the one-party state, the Cheka, terror and the ban on factions as Lenin's creations, which Stalin inherited and extended. The view that Stalin betrayed a healthier Leninism is held by Trotsky and some other writers, and Pipes rejected it.
